subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: An embryo has immotile cilia at the primitive node. Which normal event is most directly lost during establishment of the left-right axis?

options.text: A leftward nodal-fluid flow that initiates asymmetric signaling
A caudal flow that initiates neural-tube closure
A dorsal flow that separates ectoderm from mesoderm
A rightward amniotic-fluid flow that forms somites

acceptedFreeText: A leftward nodal-fluid flow that initiates asymmetric signaling
explanation: Motile cilia at the primitive node generate a directional leftward flow. That mechanical cue initiates asymmetric molecular signaling and helps establish normal left-right organ patterning.

distractorExplanations.B: Neural-tube closure is not initiated by a caudal nodal-fluid current.
distractorExplanations.C: Germ-layer separation is not the left-right symmetry-breaking function of nodal cilia.
distractorExplanations.D: Somite formation is not driven by amniotic-fluid flow, and normal nodal flow is leftward.

learningObjective: Relate motile nodal cilia to the first directional event in left-right axis specification.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: Nodal cilia are presented as the symmetry-breaking mechanism in third-week development.

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: Most of the notochord disappears as the vertebral column forms. Which adult structure normally retains notochordal tissue?

options.text: Annulus fibrosus of an intervertebral disc
Nucleus pulposus of an intervertebral disc
Posterior longitudinal ligament
Vertebral body cortical bone

acceptedFreeText: Nucleus pulposus of an intervertebral disc
explanation: The notochord provides the axial template around which vertebrae develop. Its principal adult remnant is the gelatinous nucleus pulposus in each intervertebral disc.

distractorExplanations.A: The annulus fibrosus is mesenchymal; the notochord persists centrally as the nucleus pulposus.
distractorExplanations.C: The posterior longitudinal ligament is not a notochordal remnant.
distractorExplanations.D: Vertebral bodies form around the notochord; their cortical bone is not persistent notochord.

learningObjective: Identify the adult remnant of the embryonic notochord.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: The notochord is the axis around which the vertebral column forms and persists as the nucleus pulposus.

subject: embryology
topic: Third week: gastrulation and axial patterning
prompt: During conversion of the notochordal process into the definitive notochord, a transient passage crosses the embryonic disc. Which spaces does it connect?

options.text: The chorionic cavity and maternal intervillous space
The neural tube and intraembryonic coelom
The amniotic cavity and yolk sac
The pericardial cavity and foregut

acceptedFreeText: The amniotic cavity and yolk sac
explanation: The temporary neurenteric canal passes through the primitive node and connects the amniotic cavity with the yolk sac. It normally obliterates when notochordal development is completed.

distractorExplanations.A: Those spaces are not joined by the neurenteric canal.
distractorExplanations.B: The neurenteric canal predates definitive neural-tube anatomy and does not open into the coelom.
distractorExplanations.D: This pair is unrelated to the temporary neurenteric passage.

learningObjective: Name the two cavities temporarily linked by the neurenteric canal.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: A small neurenteric canal temporarily connects the amniotic cavity and yolk sac and later obliterates.

subject: embryology
prompt: A day-20-to-30 embryo is being staged before external landmarks are reliable. Which observation from the lecture is most useful?

options.text: Count pharyngeal pouches; 38 pairs form before day 30
Measure crown-rump length; it uniquely identifies each day from 20 to 30
Count neural crest streams; 42-44 pairs form by day 30
Count paired somites; about 38 pairs form during this period and 42-44 pairs ultimately develop

acceptedFreeText: Count paired somites; about 38 pairs form during this period and 42-44 pairs ultimately develop
explanation: Somite number is a practical age criterion during the somite period. The lecture states that roughly 38 pairs form from days 20-30 and that 42-44 pairs ultimately develop.

distractorExplanations.A: Humans do not form 38 paired pharyngeal pouches.
distractorExplanations.B: The lecture specifically emphasizes somite number as a staging criterion during the somite period.
distractorExplanations.C: Neural crest streams are not counted as 42-44 serial pairs for embryonic age.

learningObjective: Use somite number as a staging clue in early embryonic development.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: About 38 pairs form during days 20-30; eventually 42-44 pairs develop, and somite count helps determine embryonic age.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which chronology of early blood-vessel formation matches the teacher's third-week lecture?

options.text: Angiogenesis begins in extraembryonic mesoderm of the yolk sac, connecting stalk, and chorion; embryonic vessels begin about two days later
Embryonic vessels arise first in paraxial mesoderm; yolk-sac vessels follow two weeks later
Angiogenesis begins simultaneously in the neural tube and amnion
Maternal vessels invade the embryo first and are remodeled into fetal endothelium

acceptedFreeText: Angiogenesis begins in extraembryonic mesoderm of the yolk sac, connecting stalk, and chorion; embryonic vessels begin about two days later
explanation: At the beginning of week 3, vessel formation starts in extraembryonic mesoderm at the yolk sac, connecting stalk, and chorion. Comparable embryonic vessel development begins roughly two days later.

distractorExplanations.B: The extraembryonic sites begin first, and the delay is about two days rather than two weeks.
distractorExplanations.C: Neither the neural tube nor the amnion is listed as the initial angiogenic site.
distractorExplanations.D: Fetal endothelial channels form from embryonic angioblasts rather than maternal vascular invasion.

learningObjective: Order extraembryonic and embryonic angiogenesis and identify the first sites.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: Angiogenesis starts in extraembryonic mesoderm at the beginning of week 3; embryonic vessels begin about two days later.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which sequence correctly describes formation of the first endothelial channels from mesenchyme?

options.text: Endoderm forms vascular tubes that recruit mesenchyme as circulating blood cells
Mesenchymal cells become angioblasts, aggregate as blood islands, develop central cavities, and flatten peripherally into endothelium
Mesenchyme first forms smooth muscle, which hollows out and becomes endothelium
Neural crest cells form erythrocytes, which arrange themselves around an empty lumen

acceptedFreeText: Mesenchymal cells become angioblasts, aggregate as blood islands, develop central cavities, and flatten peripherally into endothelium
explanation: Angioblasts aggregate into blood islands. Cavities appear inside the islands, while peripheral angioblasts flatten into endothelial cells; adjacent endothelial channels then connect by budding and fusion.

distractorExplanations.A: The endothelial channels arise from mesenchymal angioblasts, not endodermal tubes.
distractorExplanations.C: Smooth-muscle differentiation is not the blood-island sequence.
distractorExplanations.D: The early blood-island pathway uses mesenchymal angioblasts; neural crest does not form this endothelial shell.

learningObjective: Arrange the cellular steps that convert angiogenic cell clusters into endothelial channels.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: Angioblast clusters form blood islands; cavities appear and peripheral angioblasts flatten into endothelium-lined channels.

subject: embryology
prompt: By the end of the third week, paired endocardial tubes have contributed to the primordial cardiovascular system. When does the lecture place the onset of the heartbeat?

options.text: Approximately day 14
Approximately day 35
Approximately day 21 or 22
At birth, when pulmonary circulation begins

explanation: The primordial cardiovascular system becomes functional very early. The teacher slide states that blood circulates and the heart begins to beat on approximately day 21 or 22.

distractorExplanations.A: Day 14 is too early for the stated onset of the heartbeat.
distractorExplanations.B: The lecture places cardiac activity by the end of week 3, earlier than day 35.
distractorExplanations.D: The embryonic heart begins beating long before birth.

learningObjective: Recall the timing of the first embryonic heartbeat.

source.title: FORMATION OF TRILAMINAR EMBRYO.ppt
source.excerpt: By the end of week 3, blood circulates and the heart begins beating on day 21 or 22.

subject: embryology
prompt: A four-week embryo develops the first recognizable lower-respiratory primordium. Which description is correct?

options.text: A dorsal diverticulum buds from midgut mesoderm
A lateral diverticulum buds from hindgut ectoderm
A paired cavity forms within paraxial mesoderm
A ventral diverticulum buds from foregut endoderm

acceptedFreeText: A ventral diverticulum buds from foregut endoderm
explanation: At about week 4, the respiratory or laryngotracheal diverticulum appears as a ventral outgrowth of the foregut endoderm. It gives rise to the epithelial lining of the lower respiratory tract.

distractorExplanations.A: The lung bud is ventral and arises from foregut endoderm.
distractorExplanations.B: Neither the position, gut region, nor germ layer is correct.
distractorExplanations.C: The respiratory diverticulum is an endodermal foregut outgrowth, not a paraxial-mesoderm cavity.

learningObjective: Identify the timing, position, and germ-layer origin of the lung bud.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: At four weeks the lung bud appears as a ventral diverticulum in the endoderm of the foregut.

subject: embryology
prompt: The highlighted ventral outgrowth in this 25-day embryo depends on which signaling relationship for its normal position and initial development?

options.text: Retinoic acid from adjacent mesoderm upregulates TBX4 in foregut endoderm
Sonic hedgehog from endoderm suppresses all TBX4 expression in mesoderm
BMP from surface ectoderm induces PAX6 in the foregut
Nodal from the primitive node directly converts paraxial mesoderm into lung epithelium

acceptedFreeText: Retinoic acid from adjacent mesoderm upregulates TBX4 in foregut endoderm
explanation: The teacher slide links retinoic acid in adjacent mesoderm to upregulation of TBX4 in foregut endoderm. This interaction helps specify the location and appearance of the respiratory diverticulum.

distractorExplanations.B: The lecture describes retinoic-acid-dependent upregulation, not suppression of TBX4.
distractorExplanations.C: PAX6 is not the transcription factor identified for this lung-bud induction step.
distractorExplanations.D: Lower-respiratory epithelium is foregut endodermal and the cited induction uses retinoic acid and TBX4.

learningObjective: Interpret a lung-bud image using the retinoic-acid-TBX4 induction pathway.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: Retinoic acid in adjacent mesoderm causes upregulation of TBX4 in endoderm and controls lung-bud appearance and position.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which pairing correctly distinguishes epithelial from supporting-tissue origins in the developing lung?

options.text: Respiratory epithelium from splanchnic mesoderm; cartilage and smooth muscle from endoderm
Respiratory epithelium from foregut endoderm; cartilage, smooth muscle, vessels, connective tissue, and pleura from surrounding splanchnic mesoderm
All lung tissues from foregut endoderm
All lung tissues from neural crest

acceptedFreeText: Respiratory epithelium from foregut endoderm; cartilage, smooth muscle, vessels, connective tissue, and pleura from surrounding splanchnic mesoderm
explanation: Foregut endoderm forms the respiratory epithelial lining. Splanchnic mesoderm surrounding the foregut produces connective tissue, smooth muscle, cartilage, blood and lymphatic components, and the mesothelium of the pleura.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses epithelial and supporting-tissue origins.
distractorExplanations.C: Endoderm supplies epithelium, whereas surrounding splanchnic mesoderm supplies most supporting tissues.
distractorExplanations.D: Neural crest is not the common origin of lung epithelium and mesenchyme.

learningObjective: Separate endodermal epithelial derivatives from splanchnic-mesodermal lung derivatives.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: Splanchnic mesoderm around the foregut forms lung connective tissue, endothelium, smooth muscle, vessels, cartilage, lymphatics, and pleural mesothelium.

subject: embryology
prompt: Tracheoesophageal ridges fuse in the early foregut. What is the normal result of this event?

options.text: A pleuropericardial membrane separates the stomach from the duodenum
The buccopharyngeal membrane separates the trachea from the pharynx
A tracheoesophageal septum separates a ventral laryngotracheal tube from a dorsal esophagus
A dorsal mesentery separates the right and left main bronchi

acceptedFreeText: A tracheoesophageal septum separates a ventral laryngotracheal tube from a dorsal esophagus
explanation: Fusion of the tracheoesophageal ridges creates the tracheoesophageal septum. The septum partitions the foregut into a ventral laryngotracheal tube and a dorsal esophagus.

distractorExplanations.A: Pleuropericardial membranes partition thoracic cavities, not the foregut into airway and esophagus.
distractorExplanations.B: The buccopharyngeal membrane is not the longitudinal foregut partition.
distractorExplanations.D: The dorsal mesentery suspends gut structures and does not create the trachea-esophagus division.

learningObjective: Explain the normal outcome of tracheoesophageal-ridge fusion.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: Tracheoesophageal ridges form a septum that splits the foregut into esophagus and trachea with lung buds.

subject: embryology
prompt: The diagram compares major tracheoesophageal malformations. Which configuration accounts for roughly 90% of affected cases?

options.text: An isolated H-type fistula with a continuous esophagus
Pure esophageal atresia without any fistula
A blind-ending distal esophagus with only a proximal fistula
A blind-ending proximal esophagus with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula

acceptedFreeText: A blind-ending proximal esophagus with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula
explanation: The overwhelmingly common configuration is esophageal atresia with a fistulous connection between the distal esophageal segment and trachea. The proximal esophagus ends blindly.

distractorExplanations.A: The H-type fistula is much less common than atresia with a distal fistula.
distractorExplanations.B: Isolated atresia represents only a small minority of cases.
distractorExplanations.C: A proximal-only fistula is rare and is not the approximately 90% pattern.

learningObjective: Recognize the most common tracheoesophageal anomaly from a pattern diagram.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: The slide compares five atresia/fistula patterns and identifies the distal-fistula pattern as the major approximately 90% form.

subject: embryology
prompt: A newborn has a tracheoesophageal fistula. Which additional finding pair is most consistent with the association emphasized in the lecture?

options.text: Vertebral anomaly and renal anomaly
Cataract and sensorineural deafness
Polydactyly and holoprosencephaly
Pyloric stenosis and biliary atresia

explanation: VACTERL comprises vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula/esophageal atresia, renal anomalies, and limb defects.

distractorExplanations.B: These findings are not components of VACTERL.
distractorExplanations.C: This pair does not define the VACTERL association discussed with TEF.
distractorExplanations.D: Neither finding is represented by the VACTERL acronym.

learningObjective: Recognize associated anomalies represented by the VACTERL acronym.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: TEF may occur in VACTERL: vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal/esophageal, renal, and limb anomalies.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which presentation most strongly suggests esophageal atresia with a tracheoesophageal fistula during the first feeding?

options.text: Projectile nonbilious vomiting several weeks after birth
Excessive salivation with choking and cyanosis, followed by regurgitation through the mouth or nostrils
Painless jaundice with pale stools
Delayed passage of meconium with abdominal distension only

acceptedFreeText: Excessive salivation with choking and cyanosis, followed by regurgitation through the mouth or nostrils
explanation: The lecture highlights excessive salivation and the three Cs during feeding: coughing, choking, and cyanosis. Fluid may return through the mouth and nostrils, and aspiration pneumonia can follow.

distractorExplanations.A: This is more typical of pyloric stenosis and does not match the immediate three-C feeding presentation.
distractorExplanations.C: This suggests obstructive hepatobiliary disease, not a foregut connection anomaly.
distractorExplanations.D: This points toward distal intestinal obstruction rather than the feeding-associated respiratory signs of TEF.

learningObjective: Recognize the characteristic early feeding presentation of esophageal atresia with TEF.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E1.pptx
source.excerpt: Clinical features include excessive salivation, coughing/choking/cyanosis during feeding, regurgitation, and aspiration pneumonia.

subject: embryology
prompt: Experimental blockade of a mesoderm-derived signal markedly reduces airway branching. Which signal family does the teacher identify as central to this epithelial-mesenchymal interaction?

options.text: Immunoglobulins
Hemoglobins
Fibroblast growth factors
Troponins

explanation: Lung branching depends on reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal interactions. The lecture specifically identifies mesodermal fibroblast growth factor family signals as drivers of branching.

distractorExplanations.A: Immunoglobulins are not morphogens directing airway branching.
distractorExplanations.B: Hemoglobins transport gas and are not mesodermal branching signals.
distractorExplanations.D: Troponins regulate muscle contraction rather than epithelial branching morphogenesis.

learningObjective: Identify the growth-factor family emphasized in pulmonary branching morphogenesis.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Signals for branching emitted from mesoderm include members of the fibroblast growth factor family.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which sequence correctly orders the major morphologic phases of lung development after the embryonic phase?

options.text: Canalicular, pseudoglandular, alveolar, then saccular
Saccular, embryonic, pseudoglandular, then canalicular
Alveolar, saccular, canalicular, then pseudoglandular
Pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular, then alveolar

explanation: The lecture's timeline proceeds from embryonic to pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular, and alveolar development. Alveolar maturation continues after birth and through childhood.

distractorExplanations.A: The pseudoglandular phase precedes canalicular, and saccular precedes alveolar.
distractorExplanations.B: Saccular is a later fetal phase and does not precede embryonic development.
distractorExplanations.C: This is essentially the reverse of the developmental sequence.

learningObjective: Order the major phases of prenatal and early postnatal lung maturation.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: The lung-development timeline lists pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular, and alveolar phases, with postnatal continuation.

subject: embryology
prompt: A fetal lung has extensive branching through conducting airways but lacks structures adequate for gas exchange. Which phase is most likely?

options.text: Pseudoglandular phase, approximately weeks 5-16
Canalicular phase, approximately weeks 16-26
Saccular phase, mainly the sixth and seventh prenatal months
Alveolar phase, beginning late in gestation and continuing after birth

explanation: During the pseudoglandular phase the bronchial tree resembles a gland and conducting airways branch extensively, but respiratory units capable of effective gas exchange have not yet formed.

distractorExplanations.B: The canalicular phase adds respiratory bronchioles and marked vascular development, moving toward gas exchange.
distractorExplanations.C: Terminal sacs with thinning epithelium characterize the saccular phase.
distractorExplanations.D: The alveolar phase contains maturing gas-exchange units rather than only conducting airways.

learningObjective: Recognize the timing and functional limitation of the pseudoglandular lung.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: The phase timeline places pseudoglandular development after early lung-bud branching and before the canalicular phase.

subject: embryology
prompt: A lung sample from 20 weeks shows respiratory bronchioles lined mainly by cuboidal cells and a rapidly increasing capillary network. Which phase is this?

options.text: Embryonic phase
Canalicular phase
Pseudoglandular phase
Alveolar phase

explanation: The canalicular phase spans roughly weeks 16-26. Lumina enlarge, respiratory bronchioles appear, vascularity increases, and the epithelium is still substantially cuboidal.

distractorExplanations.A: The embryonic phase establishes the early lung bud and major bronchi, not respiratory bronchioles at 20 weeks.
distractorExplanations.C: Pseudoglandular development lacks the more distal respiratory bronchioles and vascular proximity described.
distractorExplanations.D: Alveolar development is later and features mature alveoli with very thin type I epithelium.

learningObjective: Identify the canalicular phase from gestational age, airway morphology, and vascular development.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: At 16-26 weeks, the canalicular-phase respiratory bronchiole is lined by cuboidal cells.

subject: embryology
prompt: During the sixth and seventh prenatal months, cuboidal cells lining terminal sacs become progressively thin. What is the key functional consequence?

options.text: The tracheoesophageal septum begins to form
The conducting bronchi lose all cartilage
The diffusion distance between air spaces and capillaries decreases
Pulmonary vessels are excluded from the terminal sacs

acceptedFreeText: The diffusion distance between air spaces and capillaries decreases
explanation: Saccular maturation thins the epithelial barrier and brings capillaries into close apposition with terminal sacs. This shortens the diffusion path needed for postnatal gas exchange.

distractorExplanations.A: Foregut partition occurs much earlier than the saccular phase.
distractorExplanations.B: Epithelial thinning in terminal sacs does not imply complete loss of bronchial cartilage.
distractorExplanations.D: Capillaries approach the thin epithelium rather than being excluded.

learningObjective: Explain why epithelial thinning in the saccular phase improves gas-exchange readiness.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: In the sixth and seventh prenatal months, cuboidal cells become very thin as terminal sacs mature.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which cell-product pair becomes especially important by the end of the sixth month of lung development?

options.text: Type I alveolar epithelial cell - cartilage matrix
Bronchial smooth-muscle cell - pulmonary surfactant
Pleural mesothelial cell - fetal hemoglobin
Type II alveolar epithelial cell - surfactant-rich phospholipid fluid

acceptedFreeText: Type II alveolar epithelial cell - surfactant-rich phospholipid fluid
explanation: Type II alveolar epithelial cells begin secreting phospholipid-rich surfactant by the end of the sixth month. Surfactant lowers surface tension at the air-alveolar interface.

distractorExplanations.A: Type I cells form the thin gas-exchange lining and do not produce cartilage.
distractorExplanations.B: Surfactant is produced by type II alveolar epithelial cells, not airway smooth muscle.
distractorExplanations.C: Pleural mesothelium neither produces fetal hemoglobin nor supplies alveolar surfactant.

learningObjective: Match pulmonary surfactant with its fetal cellular source and approximate onset.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: At the end of the sixth month, type II alveolar epithelial cells produce surfactant, a phospholipid-rich fluid.

subject: embryology
prompt: Before birth, which description best matches the fluid filling the lungs?

options.text: High chloride, little protein, some bronchial mucus, and surfactant from type II alveolar cells
High protein with no chloride and no epithelial secretions
Pure swallowed amniotic fluid with no pulmonary contribution
Maternal plasma ultrafiltrate rich in immunoglobulin

acceptedFreeText: High chloride, little protein, some bronchial mucus, and surfactant from type II alveolar cells
explanation: The prenatal lung is fluid-filled. The teacher slide characterizes that fluid as chloride-rich and protein-poor, with some mucus from bronchial glands and surfactant from type II alveolar epithelial cells.

distractorExplanations.B: The lecture specifies high chloride and little protein plus mucus and surfactant.
distractorExplanations.C: Fetal lung fluid includes secretions from bronchial glands and alveolar type II cells.
distractorExplanations.D: The stated fetal lung fluid is not described as an immunoglobulin-rich maternal ultrafiltrate.

learningObjective: Recall the principal components of fetal lung fluid before birth.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Before birth the lungs contain high-chloride, low-protein fluid plus bronchial mucus and type-II-cell surfactant.

subject: embryology
prompt: Surfactant rises especially during the final two weeks before birth. What immediate mechanical problem does adequate surfactant prevent?

options.text: Excess cartilage formation obstructing the trachea
Excess surface tension causing alveolar collapse during expiration
Failure of the diaphragm to separate from the liver
Persistent communication between the trachea and esophagus

acceptedFreeText: Excess surface tension causing alveolar collapse during expiration
explanation: Surfactant lowers surface tension at the air-liquid interface. Without it, the pressure needed to keep small alveoli open rises and alveoli tend to collapse during expiration.

distractorExplanations.A: Surfactant acts at the air-liquid interface and does not control tracheal cartilage formation.
distractorExplanations.C: Diaphragm formation is unrelated to surfactant's surface-tension effect.
distractorExplanations.D: A tracheoesophageal fistula results from foregut partitioning defects, not surfactant deficiency.

learningObjective: Explain the mechanical role of surfactant in preventing neonatal alveolar collapse.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Surfactant increases particularly in the last two weeks before birth and prevents high surface tension and expiratory alveolar collapse.

subject: embryology
prompt: A very premature infant dies with surfactant-deficiency respiratory distress syndrome. Which pathologic finding best matches the lecture?

options.text: Overexpanded alveoli lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium
Bronchi completely replaced by hyaline cartilage
Collapsed alveoli containing protein-rich fluid and numerous hyaline membranes
Pleural cavities filled only with clear transudate

acceptedFreeText: Collapsed alveoli containing protein-rich fluid and numerous hyaline membranes
explanation: In neonatal RDS, insufficient surfactant leads to widespread alveolar collapse. Protein-rich material and cellular debris form characteristic hyaline membranes along the collapsed air spaces.

distractorExplanations.A: Surfactant deficiency produces collapse, not overexpansion or keratinization.
distractorExplanations.B: Cartilage replacement is not the lesion of neonatal surfactant deficiency.
distractorExplanations.D: The defining lesion is within collapsed alveoli and includes protein-rich material and hyaline membranes.

learningObjective: Link surfactant deficiency to the characteristic pulmonary pathology of neonatal RDS.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Collapsed alveoli in RDS contain high-protein fluid, many hyaline membranes, and lamellar bodies.

subject: embryology
prompt: A pregnant patient is at high risk of imminent preterm delivery. Why are antenatal glucocorticoids given?

options.text: To close a fetal tracheoesophageal fistula
To prevent all prenatal breathing movements
To convert type I alveolar cells into bronchial cartilage
To accelerate fetal type II alveolar-cell maturation and surfactant production

acceptedFreeText: To accelerate fetal type II alveolar-cell maturation and surfactant production
explanation: Antenatal glucocorticoids accelerate maturation of the fetal lung, especially type II alveolar epithelial cells and their surfactant production, reducing morbidity and mortality from neonatal RDS.

distractorExplanations.A: Glucocorticoids do not repair an anatomic foregut-separation defect.
distractorExplanations.B: Breathing movements support lung development and are not the treatment target.
distractorExplanations.C: Glucocorticoids promote pulmonary maturation and surfactant, not cartilage metaplasia.

learningObjective: Explain the embryologic rationale for antenatal glucocorticoids in threatened preterm birth.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Maternal glucocorticoid treatment in premature labor stimulates surfactant production and reduces RDS mortality.

subject: embryology
prompt: A congenital lung lesion produces multiple cystic spaces and a honeycomb appearance on radiography. Which developmental abnormality is described?

options.text: Dilation of terminal or larger bronchi forming congenital lung cysts
Failure of the buccopharyngeal membrane to rupture
Persistence of the neurenteric canal
Absence of the septum transversum

acceptedFreeText: Dilation of terminal or larger bronchi forming congenital lung cysts
explanation: The lecture describes congenital lung cysts as dilations of terminal or larger bronchi. Multiple dilated spaces can create a honeycomb appearance on imaging.

distractorExplanations.B: That defect affects the primitive mouth and does not cause honeycomb pulmonary cysts.
distractorExplanations.C: A persistent neurenteric connection does not create dilated bronchial cysts.
distractorExplanations.D: This would disrupt diaphragm development rather than selectively dilating bronchi into cysts.

learningObjective: Connect the honeycomb radiographic pattern with the bronchial basis of congenital lung cysts.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Congenital lung cysts arise from dilation of terminal or larger bronchi and can produce a honeycomb radiographic appearance.

subject: embryology
prompt: What is the principal developmental value of breathing movements that begin before birth?

options.text: They provide the fetus's sole source of oxygen
They stimulate lung development and condition the respiratory muscles
They empty all lung fluid into the amniotic cavity
They initiate separation of the trachea from the esophagus

acceptedFreeText: They stimulate lung development and condition the respiratory muscles
explanation: Fetal breathing movements do not provide prenatal gas exchange. They mechanically stimulate pulmonary growth and prepare the respiratory musculature for effective ventilation after birth.

distractorExplanations.A: Placental exchange, not fetal air breathing, supplies oxygen before birth.
distractorExplanations.C: Most lung fluid is resorbed around birth; fetal movements do not simply empty it all prenatally.
distractorExplanations.D: Foregut partitioning occurs much earlier and is not driven by fetal breathing movements.

learningObjective: State the developmental functions of fetal breathing movements.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: Breathing movements begin before birth and stimulate lung development while conditioning respiratory muscles.

subject: embryology
prompt: Which change normally accompanies the onset of respiration at birth?

options.text: Lung fluid becomes trapped permanently inside the terminal sacs
All surfactant is washed out with the fetal lung fluid
Most lung fluid is rapidly absorbed into blood and lymphatic capillaries, leaving a thin surfactant coat on alveolar cells
Pulmonary capillaries regress because placental flow has stopped

acceptedFreeText: Most lung fluid is rapidly absorbed into blood and lymphatic capillaries, leaving a thin surfactant coat on alveolar cells
explanation: With the onset of breathing, most fetal lung fluid is rapidly cleared through pulmonary blood and lymphatic capillaries. Surfactant remains on alveolar cell membranes as a stabilizing phospholipid film.

distractorExplanations.A: Normal transition requires rapid clearance rather than permanent retention.
distractorExplanations.B: Surfactant remains as a thin phospholipid coating after fluid resorption.
distractorExplanations.D: Pulmonary perfusion increases after birth; capillaries do not regress.

learningObjective: Describe lung-fluid clearance and surfactant retention during the neonatal transition.

source.title: Embryology  of respiratory system E2.pptx
source.excerpt: At birth most lung fluid is resorbed by blood and lymph capillaries; surfactant remains as a thin phospholipid coat.

subject: embryology
prompt: This field shows very thin alveolar epithelium with capillaries closely protruding toward mature air spaces. Which developmental stage best matches the image?

options.text: Early embryonic lung-bud stage
Pseudoglandular stage
Early canalicular stage
Newborn/alveolar stage

explanation: The teacher's maturation sequence identifies the newborn lung by thin squamous type I epithelial cells and capillaries closely applied to mature alveoli. This architecture minimizes the blood-air diffusion distance.

distractorExplanations.A: The lung-bud stage lacks mature alveolar air spaces and their capillary interface.
distractorExplanations.B: Pseudoglandular lungs resemble branching glands and do not yet contain mature thin-walled alveoli.
distractorExplanations.C: Canalicular lungs are developing respiratory bronchioles and vascularity but do not yet show this mature thin alveolar-capillary arrangement.

learningObjective: Recognize a mature neonatal alveolar-capillary interface in a developmental image.

source.excerpt: At the newborn stage, thin type I alveolar epithelial cells and surrounding capillaries protrude into mature alveoli.
